Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National Food glut: Annoh-Dompreh demands answers on Buffer Stock purchases and expenditure Source : Myjoyonline.com 28 November 2026 9:19am ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Minority Chief Whip Frank Annoh-Dompreh has demanded full disclosure of the quantities of food the National Food Buffer Stock Company (NAFCO) has purchased and how much public money has been disbursed to address Ghana’s growing food glut.
The Nsawam-Adoagyiri MP is questioning the effectiveness of government interventions as farmers struggle to find buyers despite reported financial allocations to support strategic food reserves.
Delivering a statement on the floor of Parliament today, Mr Annoh-Dompreh called for urgent parliamentary scrutiny of NAFCO’s operations, expenditure, storage capacity and outstanding payments to farmers.
He cited Ghana News Agency reports indicating that NAFCO had an installed storage capacity of about 129,000 metric tonnes as of May 2026.
However, only between 40,000 and 44,000 metric tonnes were reportedly usable, despite reported support of GH¢300 million for strategic food reserves.
He also referenced a June 2026 report on the registration of 45 licensed buying companies and budgetary support comprising GH¢100 million and an additional GH¢200 million in the 2026 Budget.
“These allocations and arrangements must be assessed against actual purchases, timely payments to farmers and usable storage capacity. Announcements must produce measurable relief,” he stated.
The Minority Chief Whip wants the Minister for Food and Agriculture to provide Parliament with comprehensive data on unsold produce across the country, the number of affected farmers and the quantities purchased by NAFCO and its licensed buyers.
He also demanded details of funds disbursed, outstanding payments, current usable storage capacity and the operational status of the 45 registered buying companies.
Mr Annoh-Dompreh warned that farmers who had invested borrowed funds and scarce resources in production were struggling to recover their investments.
Many, he said, were either unable to find buyers or being offered prices below their production costs.
“A farmer who cannot sell cannot repay loans, pay workers or finance the next planting season. A trader whose goods remain unsold loses working capital, while perishable produce deteriorates.”
He warned that the failure to address the crisis could undermine future agricultural production and threaten national food security.
“If farmers respond by reducing production or abandoning agriculture, today’s glut could become tomorrow’s food shortage.”
The Minority Chief Whip called for an emergency purchase of surplus food, rehabilitation of warehouses and the prioritisation of locally produced food by public institutions, including schools, hospitals and the security services.
He further urged Parliament’s committees responsible for agriculture, finance and trade to investigate the crisis and visit affected farming communities and markets.
“The House should insist on transparent procurement, independent audit and accountability for public funds.”
Mr Annoh-Dompreh also demanded a time-bound national intervention plan with measurable targets and regular reports to Parliament.
“Our farmers do not need sympathy alone; they need buyers. Our market women need functioning markets and consumers with purchasing power.”
He urged Parliament to rise above partisan considerations and act urgently to protect agricultural livelihoods.
